newsitem.title: BELGIUM: SCANDALISED BELGIUM TO HOST CHILD ABUSE CONFERENCE.
newsitem.headline: SCANDALISED BELGIUM TO HOST CHILD ABUSE CONFERENCE.

text.p: Belgium, still rocked to its roots by revelations of child sexual abuse and murder, will next week try to ensure that it is never again allowed to threaten future generations.

A forum of experts from around the world will gather on Sunday, in the presence of Belgium's King Albert and Queen Paola, for four days of detailed discussions on how to stamp out child abuse and ensure that children's rights are respected.

"Sexual abuse of children is a major problem throughout the world, but it is little recognised," Geert Cappelaere, President of the National Commission against the Sexual Exploitation of Children, told Reuters in an interview.
"For years the problem was either hidden or ignored. In truth we still don't know enough about it," he added.

The commission was appointed by the government on August 30, barely two weeks after the rescue of two sexually abused young girls from a makeshift dungeon in the basement of a house owned by convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux, and the discovery of the bodies of two eight-year-olds at another of his houses nearby.
Less than a week later police unearthed the bodies of two teenage girls at another house linked to Dutroux, who has been charged with the murder of all four.

The commission has spent the intervening nine months drawing up a list of 25 proposals for new rules or changes in existing ones that will be debated by the four-day forum before being presented to the government by October.
Cappelaere was reluctant to reveal the details of the proposals before the conference, but he said it would be more a matter of making sure existing rules were observed than of starting a revolution.
"There are already several initiatives. We judge that it is more important to make these work rather than starting all over again from zero," he said.

The 1994 United Nations Charter for the Rights of Children is the keystone for protecting the young from the depredations of their elders, but it is still honoured more through lip service than actions, Cappelaere said.
He added that one of the main areas of abuse was in the home, making it even more difficult to identify and tackle.

"We have seen Dutroux, but we have to make it clear that these cases are much rarer than abuse by family members," he said. "It is clear that more children are sexually abused within the family than by strangers."

He said that while the whole issue was at the forefront in Belgium because of the Dutroux affair and the fact that police are still looking for other missing children, it was not a problem that was confined to the country.
"It is a world problem that needs a global solution," Capelaere, from Ghent University's Centre for Child Rights, said.

Sexual tourism, particularly for paedophile sex, is a growing problem throughout the world, particularly in Asia and Latin America, but it is one that the countries in question are finding it very hard to tackle on their own.
It was only relatively recently that Belgium changed its laws to allow it to prosecute one of its citizens who had committed a sexual crime in another country.
But at the same time sexual attitudes and practices are evolving in the west.
It appears to be a contradiction that while child rights are gaining more support, a Belgian parliamentary commission is considering a proposal to reduce the age of consent to 14 years from 16.
But the argument put forward is simple. You can't ignore reality. REUTER
